subtype: Approach: brainstorming many questions and picking one [Thinking]
passage: Paula spread a sheet of paper on the kitchen table in Valencia and wrote at the top: What do I wonder about? Ten questions followed: Do plants grow towards light? Why do ice cubes melt faster in salt water? How high does a paper plane fly? She put a tick next to those she could test with things at home, and a cross beside the ones needing special tools. Her brother Alejandro peered over. "Which will you choose?" Paula tapped the plants. "I have beans, cups and a windowsill. And I have three weeks." She circled the question and drew a little sun beside it.

qa.q: How many questions did Paula write?
What did Paula think when tapping the plant question?
qa.a: Paula thought the plant question could be tested with beans, cups and a windowsill within three weeks, so it felt possible and exciting.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Paula use to choose, and why?
qa.a: Paula could ask her teacher which questions are safe and interesting, or talk to a friend. Another view might spot a hidden problem.

qa.q: How might Alejandro see Paula's list?
qa.a: Alejandro peered over and asked which she would choose, so Alejandro seems curious and interested in the plan.

grounding: A girl writes ten questions she wonders about and picks the one she can test with home materials in the time she has.

subtype: Approach: brainstorming many questions and picking one [Thinking]
passage: In the Class 5 science club, Manoj sir gave everyone a blank page. "Write ten things you wonder about." Minakshi wrote fast: Do plants grow towards light? Why do cats purr? Can ants smell sugar? Why is the sky blue? Does music help plants? Then she stopped at ten and read them again. "Which one can I actually test?" she asked herself. Cats: they didn't have one. Sky: too hard. Music: she had no speaker. Ants: maybe, but ants run away. Light: two pots, a window and a cupboard, all at home. She had four weeks. She circled question one. Manoj sir looked over her shoulder. "Why that one?" "Because I can do it at home, and it'll be ready in time."

qa.q: How many things did Manoj sir ask everyone to write?
qa.a: He asked them to write ten things they wonder about.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel when she circled question one?
qa.a: She felt sure and pleased, having thought through each question and found one she could really do.

qa.q: What else could Minakshi check before starting, and why?
qa.a: She could check how long plants take to bend towards light, so she knows the four weeks is enough.

qa.q: How does Minakshi's choice look to Manoj sir?
qa.a: Manoj sir is curious, and her clear reason shows him she has thought about time and materials.

grounding: It shows a girl writing ten questions she wonders about and picking the one she can test with materials at home in the time she has.

subtype: Approach: brainstorming many questions and picking one [Thinking]
passage: My sister Kavitha had a science fair coming up, and I watched her spend Saturday morning on the floor of our room with a notebook. She wrote question after question. I read some upside down: "Why does ice float? Do plants like light? Can a spider smell?" She had ten. Then she started crossing them out. I don't know what she was thinking, but she kept looking around the room, at the window, at the cupboard, at Amma's plant pots on the balcony. By lunch she had only one left: "Do plants lean towards light?" She went to Amma and asked for two small pots. Our neighbour Naveen uncle gave her some bean seeds. By evening the pots were ready.

qa.q: Who gave Kavitha some bean seeds?
qa.a: Naveen uncle, the neighbour, gave her some bean seeds.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be thinking as she looks around the room?
qa.a: She may be working out what materials she has at home, feeling focused and hopeful, though the sibling can only guess.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do to choose between two good questions?
qa.a: She could ask which one can finish in time before the fair, since time matters as much as materials.

qa.q: How does the morning look to the sibling watching?
qa.a: The sibling sees a messy list slowly shrink to one clear question, and is curious enough to read it upside down.

grounding: It shows a girl brainstorming ten questions and picking the one she can test at home in the time available.
